scams.name: Taxi Bill-Switch and Counterfeit Change
scams.description:
You flag a taxi along the waterfront in El Rodadero or outside a hotel in the Centro Histórico. The driver quotes a fare of around 10,000–15,000 pesos, which sounds reasonable, and the ride proceeds without incident.

At payment, you hand over a 20,000-peso note. The driver turns briefly away, then holds up a 2,000-peso note: "You only gave me 2,000." He has palmed your real bill and substituted a smaller one in a smooth sleight-of-hand. In the counterfeit variant, you pay with a 50,000-peso note and he returns it saying it is fake or he has no change — the next day a shopkeeper tells you the bill is counterfeit. The driver kept your genuine note.

Pay taxis with exact-denomination notes and announce the amount aloud as you hand it over. Pre-negotiating the fare, carrying small bills (5,000 and 10,000 peso notes), and using ride-hailing apps like InDriver or Didi removes the cash-handling opportunity entirely.
scams.avoidance: Carry small bills (5,000 and 10,000 peso notes) and pay with exact change whenever possible State the denomination out loud as you hand it to the driver: 'Here is twenty thousand pesos' Agree on the fare before entering the taxi and have the exact amount ready Use ride-hailing apps like InDriver, Didi, or Uber where payment is handled digitally Familiarize yourself with Colombian bill denominations and security features before arriving — check returned bills for watermarks
scams.location: Taxis throughout Santa Marta, especially outside hotels in El Rodadero, the Centro Histórico, and near Parque de los Novios at night
scams.tldr: Santa Marta taxi drivers running a bill-switch con palm your large peso note and claim you gave a smaller one — or return your genuine bill as counterfeit — costing you 18,000–50,000 pesos per ride.

scams.name: Fake Police Document Inspection
scams.description:
You are walking near the Centro Histórico or Parque de los Novios when two men in uniforms that closely resemble Colombian National Police attire step into your path. They flash badges quickly — too fast to read a badge number — and say they are conducting a random check for counterfeit currency.

One officer takes your passport and flips through it while the other asks to see your wallet. As he "inspects" your bills, he palms cash between his fingers while appearing to hold each note up to the light. They hand everything back, issue a formal-looking receipt, and tell you to collect your funds at the police station. At the station, real officers confirm no such check was ever authorized — the cash is gone.

Real Colombian police do not conduct street wallet inspections for counterfeit bills — this demand alone identifies the encounter as a scam. If approached, keep your wallet in your pocket, request to walk together to the nearest official police station, and call 123 to verify the officer's identity. Genuine officers will comply; impersonators will not.
scams.avoidance: Leave your passport at the hotel safe and carry only a photocopy of the photo page and entry stamps If approached by supposed police, politely request to see their official photo ID and badge number Suggest walking to the nearest police station to verify their identity — real officers will agree, scammers will not Never hand over your wallet — if asked for ID, hold it yourself and let them look at it in your hands Call 123 (Colombian police emergency) to verify any officer's identity before complying with demands
scams.location: Streets around the Centro Histórico, Parque de los Novios, walkways near Taganga, and roads near popular tourist sites
scams.tldr: Men in convincing police-style uniforms approach tourists near Parque de los Novios, demand to inspect documents and wallets for counterfeit bills, and pocket cash during the "inspection" — leaving victims with a worthless receipt.

scams.name: Beach Distraction Theft
scams.description:
You lay your towel and bag on the sand at Playa El Rodadero or Taganga Beach and walk into the water. The beach is busy and the mood is relaxed. A vendor or passerby drifts near your belongings without drawing attention.

An accomplice then creates a small scene — a beach ball lands near your bag, a radio suddenly blares, or someone calls out to nearby sunbathers. In the moment you glance up or other beachgoers look away, the first person rifles through your bag and takes your phone, wallet, and camera. In a second variant, someone wades out to sell you drinks while their partner works the shore.

Take only what you can carry into the water and lock everything else in your hotel safe before reaching the beach. When swimming with a partner, take turns in the water so someone is always watching. At Tayrona or Taganga, carry only day-trip cash and a cheap secondary phone.
scams.avoidance: Never leave valuables unattended on the beach — bring only what you need for the day and leave everything else at the hotel Use a waterproof phone pouch that you can take into the water with you Take turns swimming with a travel companion so someone always watches the belongings Use a portable beach safe or lockbox that you can secure to a fixed object like a beach chair At Tayrona Park or Taganga, bring only essentials: cash for food, a cheap phone, and sunscreen
scams.location: Playa El Rodadero, Taganga Beach, Playa Blanca, and beach areas around Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona
scams.tldr: Coordinated two- to three-person teams work Santa Marta's beaches — one creates a distraction while another rifles through unattended bags, typically stealing phones, wallets, and cameras in under thirty seconds.

scams.name: Scopolamine (Devil's Breath) Drink Spiking
scams.description:
You are at a bar in El Rodadero and an attractive person strikes up a friendly conversation. The venue is loud and social; the interaction feels ordinary. They offer to buy you a drink or suggest a toast.

The drink is spiked with scopolamine, known locally as burundanga — a colorless, odorless substance derived from the borrachero plant. Within minutes you feel unusually compliant and disoriented. Hours later you wake up in your hotel room with no memory of the intervening period. Your phone, wallet, watch, and laptop are gone. The drug can be slipped into a drink, placed on a business card, or blown as powder toward the face.

Never leave your drink unattended or accept a beverage from someone you just met at a bar. If you feel suddenly dizzy after even one drink, alert a trusted friend immediately and move to a safe location. Avoid bringing strangers back to your hotel, and meet app contacts for the first time in busy public spaces during daylight.
scams.avoidance: Never accept drinks from strangers and never leave your drink unattended — get a new one if you stepped away Avoid bringing strangers to your hotel room, especially people met at bars or through dating apps Go out with trusted friends and watch out for each other — if someone seems suddenly out of it, get them to safety immediately Use drink covers or bottle toppers to prevent anything being dropped into your beverage If you feel suddenly disoriented after a drink, tell a trusted person immediately and get to a safe location
scams.location: Bars and nightclubs in El Rodadero, late-night establishments in the Centro Histórico, and encounters initiated through dating apps
scams.tldr: Strangers at bars in El Rodadero — or contacts from dating apps — spike tourists' drinks with scopolamine (burundanga), a colorless drug that induces compliance and memory loss, then rob them of phones, cash, watches, and laptops.

scams.name: Overpriced Unofficial Tour Guide
scams.description:
You arrive at the entrance to Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona and a well-presented man approaches, offering a private guided tour for 80,000 pesos. He knows the park's layout, names the beaches correctly, and projects confidence. The price sounds fair before you have checked the official alternatives.

Once inside, the guide provides minimal commentary, spends most of the trail on his phone, and rushes to the beaches in under an hour. He declares the tour over at the first beach and walks off. Self-guided park entry costs only 20,000 pesos; licensed guides through official channels charge 50,000–60,000. For the Lost City trek, unauthorized operators are even more problematic — they lack the permits required by Colombia's tourism authority, and some have left clients stranded mid-trail.

Book the Lost City trek only through one of the four licensed operators: Expotur, Wiwa Tour, Turcol, or Magic Tour. For Tayrona, purchase entry at the official booth and hire guides only from the accredited desk inside the park entrance. Check TripAdvisor or GetYourGuide reviews before you arrive so you know the correct price and licensed operators for any tour in the region.
scams.avoidance: Book tours through licensed agencies with verified reviews on TripAdvisor, Google, or GetYourGuide For the Lost City trek, only book with one of the few licensed operators (Expotur, Wiwa Tour, Turcol, or Magic Tour) Ask for official guide credentials and verify them with the tourism office if in doubt Get a written agreement including the itinerary, inclusions, and refund policy before paying Research the standard price for any tour before arriving so you can spot both overcharging and suspiciously low offers
scams.location: Outside the entrance to Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona, Minca coffee farm tours, Lost City (Ciudad Perdida) trek departures, and around Santa Marta's harbor
scams.tldr: Unlicensed touts at Tayrona National Park and Ciudad Perdida trek departures offer guided tours at inflated or artificially low prices, then deliver minimal service — charging up to four times the cost of the official licensed option.

scams.name: Bird Poop and Bracelet Distraction Theft
scams.description:
You are walking through the Centro Histórico near the cathedral or along the Parque de los Novios promenade. The streets are busy with tourists and vendors. Someone taps your shoulder, points urgently at your jacket, and says "bird poop!" — a white smear has appeared from nowhere.

A second helpful person immediately materializes with napkins, dabbing at the stain and apologizing. While your eyes are fixed on your jacket and your hands are busy with the mess, a third person behind you slips a hand into your pocket or unzips your bag. The bracelet variant works on the same principle: a street vendor ties a colorful bracelet on your wrist as a "free gift," then demands 50,000–100,000 pesos while accomplices work your pockets during the argument.

If someone points out a sudden stain, do not stop — keep walking to a safe, open area before inspecting your clothing. Decline any unsolicited bracelet or gift firmly and without stopping. In the Centro Histórico, carry your bag on your front and keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket.
scams.avoidance: If someone points out a stain, do not stop — walk away to a safe area before inspecting your clothing Do not accept 'free' bracelets, flowers, or gifts from strangers — decline firmly and keep walking Wear your bag on your front in the Centro Histórico and keep your phone in a zipped inner pocket Travel with a companion when possible so someone can watch your back during unexpected interactions Be especially alert near the cathedral and Parque de los Novios where these teams operate most actively
scams.location: Centro Histórico around the cathedral, Parque de los Novios, beachfront promenades, and busy pedestrian streets near Rodadero
scams.tldr: Teams of two to four people work the Centro Histórico using staged "bird poop" spills or unsolicited bracelet ties to create a distraction, then pick pockets or unzip bags during the confusion.

scams.name: Attempted Knifepoint Robbery Near Historic Center
scams.description:
You leave a restaurant or bar near Parque de los Novios after dark and take a short cut through a narrower side street toward your hotel. The main squares are well-lit and patrolled, but a single block off the tourist corridor the street is quiet and unlit.

Two young men step out of a doorway or shadow. One brandishes a knife and demands your phone, wallet, and watch. The robbery is fast — under a minute — and resistance prompts the threat to escalate. Victims who hesitate or argue have had phones snatched and been pushed.

Use a ride-hailing app like InDriver or Uber for any journey after dark, even for distances that feel walkable. Stick to the well-lit corridors around Carrera 1 and the Parque de los Novios when on foot at night, and ask your hotel which specific streets are safe before heading out. Leave watches, jewelry, and visible cameras in your room.
scams.avoidance: Never walk on side streets in Santa Marta after dark — use Uber, InDriver, or a hotel-arranged taxi even for short distances Stick to well-lit, well-trafficked streets like Carrera 1 and the Parque de los Novios area when out at night Do not wear expensive jewelry, watches, or visible electronics when walking around the city If confronted, hand over your belongings without resistance — nothing is worth your safety Ask your hotel which specific streets are safe to walk at night and which to avoid
scams.location: Side streets off the Centro Histórico at night, dark streets near Taganga, and poorly lit areas between bars and hotels
scams.tldr: Robbers targeting tourists on unlit side streets near the Centro Histórico and Taganga approach in pairs — one with a knife — and demand phones, wallets, and watches, completing the robbery in under a minute.
